papers.title: Exponential Convergence of the Lifted Gradient Flow of the Bass Functional
papers.summary: We establish multidimensional exponential convergence of the lifted Bass gradient flow in martingale optimal transport. Let $μ\le_{cx}ν$ be an irreducible pair, with compact convex target support, source support strictly inside the target support, and target density bounded above and bounded away from zero almost everywhere on its interior. For every bounded $σ(X)$-measurable initial state, the flow converges exponentially in $L^2$ to the global minimizer with the prescribed mean, and the functional value gap decays exponentially. Both bounds hold at every nonnegative time with the exact initial errors as prefactors. The quantitative step is strong convexity on sets with a common $L^\infty$ bound and a fixed mean. We prove it by interpolating entropic endpoint potentials, using two conditional copies to cancel the unknown potential increment, and obtaining a Hessian lower bound uniform in the regularization parameter. Removing the regularization yields curvature for the original functional; the known qualitative theory supplies a common bound for the orbit. This extends the one-dimensional exponential-convergence result of Backhoff-Veraguas, Pammer, and Schachermayer. The main result is formalized in Lean 4. AI was used in preparing the paper (see Section 8).
papers.comment: 38 pages, 8 figures (4 in each language). Complete English version followed by the Russian version. Lean 4 verification sources included as ancillary material

papers.title: Comparing tail forecasts: the number of exceedances is the sample size
papers.summary: When two forecasts of a tail, such as prediction intervals at high coverage, extreme quantiles or expected shortfall (ES), are compared by a consistent score, the score difference is known in advance except on the days on which the outcome falls beyond a forecast. The number of these exceedances, not the number of observations, is the effective sample size. For intervals at miscoverage level $α$, the number of observations a comparison needs grows like $1/α$ while the number of exceedances it needs does not, and for some pairs of forecasts no test can do better. A confidence sequence that is valid at all times and needs no distributional assumption attains this rate; Hoeffding-type procedures, calibrated by the range of the score difference, need $1/α$ times more. When exceedances are scarce, the Diebold-Mariano test declares the less conservative forecaster better with at least, asymptotically, the probability of observing no exceedance, whichever forecaster is actually better; the usual small-sample corrections do not remove this, while a bootstrap-t version largely does. For (value-at-risk, ES) forecasts, a less conservative ES can be shown without assumptions to be worse on the days on which it is less conservative, but never to be better without an assumption on the loss tail. In 250-day windows of 97.5% forecasts for seven stock indices, 18.4% of significant Diebold-Mariano results favouring the less conservative model contradict the ranking on the remaining days, against 6.9% of those favouring the more conservative one.
papers.comment: 23 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23770670

papers.title: The Generalised Kessler Syndrome and the Persian Gulf
papers.summary: The term Kessler syndrome was coined for a runaway orbital cascade creating a high-density debris field. The idea is generalised and applied to supply chains. An additive channel enables failures to generate further failures; a subtractive channel erodes the capacity to contain and restore. When damage outpaces repair, failure becomes irreversible and the system settles into a new state. Supplies connect the theory to its application. Stocks insulate subsystems from one another, and their exhaustion exposes dependencies. For the Persian Gulf states, restrictions on maritime supplies from spring 2026 are inadequately compensated by air and road transport alternatives. This depletes inventories unevenly across products and impairs the functioning of the logistics system itself. Throughput optimisation builds fragility everywhere; the Gulf is where it is becoming visible, with the Strait of Hormuz restriction as the trigger. Formulated as a Kelly portfolio allocation under a weakest-link payoff, the optimal strategy concentrates resources on the lagging rather than the leading inputs.

papers.title: Strong rate for one-dimensional driftless continuous strict local martingales
papers.summary: For one-dimensional strict local martingales of the form $\mathrm{d} X_t=σ(X_t) \mathrm{d} W_t$ starting from $X_{0}=x_{0}>0$, we prove the strong rate $\mathbb{E}\left[|X^h_N-X_T|\right] \lesssim h^{\min\{θα,\frac{1}{2}\}}$ for a discrete scheme~$X^h$ truncated at a level $h^{-α}$, with time step~$h$, as $h\downarrow 0$, where~$θ$ depends on the truncation property. For the CEV model $σ(x)\equiv x^{1+γ}$ in particular, the rate is~$\frac{1}{2}$ for any $γ\in (0,1)$ (up to a logarithmic pre-factor at $γ=\frac{1}{2}$).

papers.title: Information Flow and Market Risk: Transformer-Based Evidence on Sentiment and Volatility Dynamics
papers.summary: This study examines whether transformer-based financial news sentiment improves equity volatility forecasts beyond conventional market-based predictors. Using data for eleven US stocks, we compare volatility persistence models with specifications incorporating the VIX, AAII investor sentiment, and news sentiment extracted using ModernFinBERT. The forecasting target is annualized volatility constructed from future averages of trailing 252-session Yang-Zhang estimates, evaluated at horizons of 1, 5, and 22 trading days. Models are assessed through walk-forward testing with expanding and rolling estimation windows, fixed initial hyperparameter selection, and statistical comparisons accounting for multiple testing and serial dependence. Results show that a naive persistence benchmark achieves the lowest average QLIKE loss at all horizons. Although HAR-VIX produces the largest number of individual forecasting wins under expanding windows, it does not achieve the lowest mean loss. Adding text-based sentiment improves HAR forecasts in only two of 33 expanding-window comparisons, and neither improvement remains statistically significant under longer HAC bandwidths. A blinded audit of 2,700 news texts further characterizes the agreement and confidence patterns of ModernFinBERT classifications. The findings do not establish a general incremental forecasting advantage from transformer-based news sentiment. They highlight the importance of strong benchmarks, temporal alignment, robust inference, and careful evaluation of text-derived predictors.

papers.title: Early-Buyer Groups and Fast-Wallet Teams on a Bonding-Curve Launchpad: A Prospective Measurement Study of pump.fun on Solana
papers.summary: We study coordinated groups of wallets on a bonding-curve launchpad (pump.fun on Solana), using a complete record of 200\,443 token launches, 15\,854\,121 curve trades and 51\,025\,958 SOL transfers over 88.3 hours. A prospective, multi-channel discovery procedure (co-buying, shared funding, joint signing, transfers, consolidation) yields 23\,710 wallet groups. Without ground-truth labels we validate them by out-of-sample link prediction, independent non-trading links and a comparison with naive co-buy clustering at equal numbers of flagged tokens: raw clustering collapses into one giant component, yet it ranks tokens at least as well as the groups, so the value of the structure is descriptive. Group activity is highly concentrated and splits into serial creators and long-lived rings of early buyers. Known members buy earlier than other buyers of the same token and extract more cash than an activity-matched placebo set, while late buyers' net cash flow is negative; tokens with members show a pump-like price path, but the contrast vanishes when controls are restricted to comparable tokens, so we report it as an association. A follower entering at the earliest group signal loses money out of sample in all 32 configurations and does no better than random entry. A few pools of tens to over a hundred fast wallets are associated with a two- to four-fold higher chance of reaching 20 SOL, also within creators, with a smaller excess at 60 SOL and none for graduation; on a final hold-out the team rules keep a precision of about one half to three quarters, yet many signals arrive when the curve already holds 20 SOL, one team supplies most of them, and they add no information beyond early curve state. We also document evaluation errors that turn the same data into apparent profit.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders as Implicit Diversification Regularisers for Cross-Sectional Cryptocurrency Returns
papers.summary: Factor models are central to asset pricing and portfolio construction, but neural factors are often difficult to interpret, and their effect on portfolio risk is unclear. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) may address both concerns by describing daily returns across many assets with only a few active features. We ask whether this sparse representation produces stable financial factors and better-diversified portfolios. We study cryptocurrency returns, use equities as a secondary test, and compare the SAE with common benchmarks in a time-ordered evaluation. We find consistently lower volatility in SAE portfolios and link this result to lower correlations among the selected assets. However, the SAE does not outperform a simple contrarian strategy on risk-adjusted return, and its factor identities are not stable across training runs. Our contribution is to show that sparse coding can support portfolio diversification, while clearly separating this risk effect from claims about alpha or stable factor identities.

papers.title: Persistence of Bounded Rationality in Financial Markets: An Evolutionary Game-Theoretic Model
papers.summary: Classical theory predicts that irrational traders lose money to rational traders and are eventually driven out of the market. Yet noise trading, herding, and heuristic trading persist even in highly developed markets. We model a financial market as an ecology of two trading-behavior types, relatively rational (R) and boundedly rational (N), whose composition evolves under replicator dynamics according to relative performance. Each type's fitness depends on the share of the other type and on frictions. When the interaction is complementary, that is, rational traders profit from the mispricing created by boundedly rational traders while the latter benefit from the liquidity and price correction supplied by the former, and when the difference in frictions is moderate, a unique interior composition exists and is globally asymptotically stable: bounded rationality persists endogenously. When the interaction is antagonistic, the same point becomes a tipping threshold between two one-type regimes. Comparative statics show that lowering the costs of disciplined trading, as algorithmic and AI-based trading does, shifts the composition toward rational trading continuously but does not eliminate bounded rationality unless the cost advantage exceeds an explicit threshold.

papers.title: Mean Field Games of Optimal Trading with an SPDE Model of the Limit Order Book
papers.summary: We develop a mean field game model for optimal trading in which the interaction among traders is mediated by the dynamics of the limit order book. The bid- and ask-side order densities are modelled as stochastic processes with values in infinite-dimensional function spaces that solve stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) with stochastic order submission rates and multiplicative infinite-dimensional noise. This extends an existing limit order book framework to capture the aggregate impact of the strategic traders on the order densities. Trading activity affects the order densities, which determine the market depths near the best quotes and hence the mid-price, and the mid-price in turn affects the traders' decisions. We establish the well-posedness and regularity of the resulting density-price system and use it to formulate an $N$-player optimal trading game in which the traders' market orders enter the book through their aggregate order flow. We then study the corresponding mean field game as the number of traders tends to infinity, characterize the mean field equilibrium as a fixed point of the associated consistency condition, and prove its existence and uniqueness under suitable conditions. Finally, we show that the mean field equilibrium induces an $ε_N$-Nash equilibrium for the finite-player game, with $ε_N=O(N^{-1/2})$, and provide a numerical illustration of the equilibrium dynamics.

papers.title: Right Numbers, Wrong Questions: Evaluating LLMs on Underspecified Financial Queries
papers.summary: Financial assistants answer questions that sound factual but depend on what the user leaves unsaid: what a data figure measures, which product variant is meant, and the investor's situation and the rules that apply. An assistant that ignores these can still answer with a real number from its data, one that answers a different question. We call this frame collapse. We study it in Indian mutual funds, where product variants and tax rules are formally defined, so the correct answer can be computed for every reading. One study tests each challenge. Given an ambiguously labelled figure, models used it, often under the user's label. Given every alternative labelled, they listed them all, but the layout decided which came first. Missing a fact about the investor, weaker agents assumed a default or an outdated tax rule; requiring the fact did not guarantee its use. Because such answers match their data, checks against the data pass them. An AI judge caught mislabelled figures only when told what each field means, and still passed answers that silently chose another reading. We show how these failures arise, not how often, and propose controls for financial assistants.

papers.title: Calibration of Passive Market Impact with a Queue-Sensitive Propagator Model
papers.summary: We develop a framework for calibrating passive market impact, defined as the price response to liquidity-providing limit orders, in contrast to the impact of liquidity-consuming market orders. We build on the model of Ouazzani Chahdi, Rosenbaum, and Szymanski (arxiv:2412.07461), which combines Hawkes-driven market-order flow with queue-reactive limit-order and cancellation dynamics. Within this model, we show that the price decomposes into a universal propagator term driven by signed order-flow imbalance and a state-dependent correction that captures the dependence of price sensitivity on volume at the best quotes. This decomposition links limit-order-book microstructure to standard propagator models and yields a regression on two observable signals: the propagator signal and the queue-weighted order-flow imbalance. We calibrate the model on high-frequency order-book data and find that the passive-impact term explains substantial variation in prices beyond the classical propagator, improving both model fit and the accuracy of predicted impact curves.

papers.title: Negative Convexity in Pass-Through MBS: Mechanisms and Conditions
papers.summary: This paper investigates the mechanisms and conditions underlying negative convexity in pass-through mortgage-backed securities (MBSs) backed by fixed-rate mortgages. We first derive an exact decomposition of MBS prices into three components: the present value of interest-rate-independent cash flows, the present value of principal repaid early through interest-rate-dependent prepayments, and an interest rate option component capturing the reduction in future cash flows due to prepayments. Under a first-order approximation, the latter two components resemble portfolios of floorlets and Asian-style interest rate options, respectively. We then apply a cumulant expansion to derive closed-form valuation approximations under the one-factor Hull--White model. Numerical results show that including the second cumulant improves accuracy relative to a first-cumulant approximation. Building on the price decomposition, we decompose duration and convexity into component-level contributions and express the condition for negative convexity in terms of their second-order interest rate sensitivities. Finally, phase diagrams across interest rate levels and refinancing sensitivities identify the regions where negative convexity occurs and the corresponding sign boundaries. The negative-convexity region expands as the long-run mean of refinancing sensitivity increases. Negative convexity can arise even when no refinancing incentive exists initially, while its magnitude may vary nonmonotonically with the interest rate level. These findings explain negative MBS convexity through the sensitivities of its price components and quantitatively characterize the conditions governing its occurrence.

papers.title: CADENCE: Distributional Next-Transaction Forecasting for Business Cash-Flow Underwriting
papers.summary: Recurring cash flows are the backbone of cash-flow underwriting: they separate durable revenue from one-off deposits, expose standing obligations, and ultimately determine ability to pay. For small businesses, recurrence is both indispensable and hard to estimate, because much of their income arrives as ambiguous transfers, most payment streams are short, and schedules follow calendar conventions that frequency-domain methods treat as noise. We present CADENCE, Calendar-Aware Distributional Event Network for Cash-Flow Estimation, a compact causal Transformer that treats each transaction as a token and predicts the amount and a full, nonparametric timing distribution of every cash flow's next payment. Inheriting transaction semantics from an external labeler and a frozen text encoder keeps CADENCE compact yet general across the long tail of small-business counterparties, while predicting a calibrated distribution rather than an opaque embedding makes its outputs interpretable enough to feed existing underwriting models and power credit decisions. Ablations confirm the role of each design choice, with counterparty semantics driving recall on short histories, calendar inputs driving timing accuracy, and no-event supervision driving precision. Against the production FFT baseline, CADENCE improves one-day timing accuracy by 93.3% and next-event F1 by 6.7%, while producing calibrated distributions that serve directly as a confidence gate for downstream decisions. In an end-to-end credit evaluation on production applications, replacing FFT recurrence features with CADENCE features raises KS by 4.8%, raises the approval rate at a fixed loss rate by 18.2%, and lowers the loss rate at a fixed approval rate by 13.1%.

papers.title: What Language Models Add to Healthcare-Equity Rankings, and What They Could Have Known
papers.summary: In healthcare equities, much of what moves a single name arrives as text: filings, trial and regulatory records, news and analyst commentary. We evaluate how screened non-market features and language-model representations improve market-based equity rankings for US healthcare firms over 2020-2025. Adding balance-sheet and attention features improves the resulting hybrid's price- and liquidity-neutral rank information coefficient (IC) at one, three and twelve months. At twelve months, neutral IC rises from 0.063 to 0.093, a 48% increase, while raw IC rises from 0.289 to 0.298. Language models contribute most clearly at three months: among company-months with scientific-text coverage, a current embedding model raises the hybrid's neutral IC from 0.046 to 0.056. This increment is nominally significant (t = 2.8; paired 95% bootstrap interval [+0.006, +0.015]) and remains exploratory. A larger post hoc gain occurs in months containing trial or regulatory records, consistent with text complementing prices and financial statements at that horizon. Across all text, pre-2020 and current representations yield small positive three-month increments in both neutral and raw IC but no established twelve-month gain. Much of their ranking performance survives within-company time shuffling, consistent with a persistent company component. Rater-cutoff comparisons find negligible pre-cutoff advantages for current models over the pre-2020 rater at one and three months that do not shrink after the cutoffs; twelve-month hindsight attribution remains inconclusive. At twelve months, balance-sheet signals lead after rallies and in volatile markets, while attention leads after declines. Retrospective state-dependent blending improves on a static blend without an established advantage over the full hybrid. Results apply to a survivor-only sector sample and remain unadjusted for the full exploratory search.
papers.comment: 27 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the AI4F Workshop, ACM ICAIF 2026, Milan

papers.title: Contemporaneous Transmission Networks and Systemic Risk in European Banking
papers.summary: We study how contemporaneous equity-return transmission shapes systemic exposure among 51 listed European banks. Using a recursive non-Gaussian network model on volatility-standardized returns, we construct two market-capitalization-weighted measures based on direct and indirect transmission effects: the Systemic Impact Score (SIS), capturing a bank's potential influence on other institutions, and the Systemic Vulnerability Score (SVS), capturing its exposure to disturbances originating elsewhere. The fitted network reveals distinct transmitting and receiving roles, highlighting differences between institutions with substantial outward influence and those with high incoming sensitivity. Receiving roles are generally more reproducible than transmitting roles across repeated network discovery, and selected connections remain informative about lower-tail dependence in subsequent observations. Volatility standardization substantially reduces detected dependence among recovered shocks, although the full-sample model does not satisfy the designated criterion for supporting shock independence. Alternative recursive orderings also yield comparable directional tail asymmetries, limiting the extent to which these patterns validate a particular ordering. The results provide complementary measures of model-implied systemic transmission and vulnerability, with explicit attention to uncertainty and identification limits

papers.title: Optimal Order Placement under a State-Dependent Hawkes Process Limit Order Book model
papers.summary: We study optimal quote placement for a market maker facing order flow modeled by a state-dependent Hawkes process. A block-based linear demand specification links market-order counts to execution volumes, providing the demand moments required by a continuous time discrete state dynamic programming formulation. Under a quadratic terminal inventory penalty, we characterize inventory-dependent quotes and derive backward recursions for the coefficients of a quadratic value function. Numerical experiments using LOBSTER data examine quote distributions, inventory exposure, and terminal wealth. The implemented strategy yields higher aggregate terminal wealth than fixed-spread benchmarks at one and three ticks, but lower wealth than the two-tick benchmark. These results illustrate the framework's numerical implementation and distinguish terminal-wealth comparisons from evaluation under the inventory-penalized objective.

papers.title: An Application of Geometric Riemannian Pricing Algorithm for Valuing Catastrophe Bonds in Incomplete Markets: Market-Consistent Financial Entropy and the Split of Frequency and Severity Risk Premia
papers.summary: This paper presents a framework for pricing catastrophe (CAT) bonds in incomplete markets through Riemannian geometric optimization of financial entropy. We formulate pricing-measure selection as a maximum financial entropy problem on a finite-dimensional manifold of equivalent measures, parameterized by the non-hedgeable market prices of catastrophe frequency and severity risk, with discounting fixed by the default-free term structure. Since unconstrained entropy maximization recovers the physical measure, we incorporate observed secondary-market spreads, both pooled and date by date. For a compound Poisson-generalized Pareto loss model with Wang distortion, we derive closed-form expressions for financial entropy and the Riemannian metric. We show that CAT bond prices depend on frequency and severity premia primarily through the risk-neutral trigger intensity, making the two premia unidentifiable from market data alone; the entropy criterion resolves this ambiguity. Using a hypothetical earthquake CAT bond calibrated to quarterly spreads of Golden State Re II Ltd. (Series 2014-1), we obtain risk-neutral trigger intensities of 6.58 to 10.45 times the physical intensity (9.20 pooled and 18.26 at the end of 2015). The model-implied risk multiple aligns with the market spread-to-expected-loss ratio (8.87 versus 8.81 at issuance). The minimal-entropy measure attributes 53.5% to 63.7% of the log risk multiple to frequency risk, reflecting the selection principle rather than market identification. Finally, equating the coupon with the quoted spread understates the risk multiple by approximately half.

papers.title: A Deep Learning-Driven Operator Splitting Scheme for Free Boundary Problems: An Application to American Option Pricing in Incomplete Markets
papers.summary: This paper proposes a deep learning-driven operator splitting scheme for high-dimensional free-boundary problems, with American option pricing as a representative application. In a market with proportional transaction costs, a stochastic liquidity risk with an empirically validated nonlinear drift based on S&P 500 data, and two-factor stochastic volatility, the pricing problem takes the form of a five-dimensional highly nonlinear variational inequality. The proposed scheme decomposes this variational inequality at each time layer into an elliptic continuation equation approximated by a physics-informed neural network and a closed-form projection step enforcing the early-exercise constraint. A conditional $\ell^\infty$ stability bound is derived under stated resolvent and Lipschitz assumptions. The scheme is validated against finite-difference and least-squares Monte Carlo benchmarks, and both the option prices and the learned exercise boundary show close agreement with the reference solutions. Sensitivity analyses with respect to the key model parameters are also reported.

papers.title: Depositing More Should Not Earn Less: Supplier Income Monotonicity and Rate Curve Design in Pooled Lending Markets
papers.summary: In utilization dependent interest rate models, adding liquidity can reduce a supplier's total interest income even as the supplier's balance increases. A supplier holding a fraction $α$ of final pool supply keeps income nondecreasing with a marginal deposit exactly when $α(1+η)\leq1$, where $η$ is the elasticity of the borrow rate with respect to utilization. When the condition fails, the supplier can instead raise its income by withdrawing, which pushes utilization further up. On two public Drift markets, a lender held more of the pool than the curve protected in at least one hour in nine on SOL and one in thirteen on USDC. A protocol turns this into a design constraint by choosing, at each utilization, the largest supplier share it intends to protect. That choice caps the elasticity, and integrating the cap describes every admissible curve. Protecting the same share at every utilization gives a power law boundary, and protecting every fresh depositor gives a hyperbolic one. On a multiple kink USDT market, compliant repairs can lower or raise supplier income, because the constraint governs how income responds to a deposit and not the price level.

papers.title: Simple Portfolios that Deliver Consistent Decent Returns
papers.summary: Portfolio construction has been studied extensively in both academia and industry. Its applications range from pension funds and hedge funds to private savings. The academic literature centers on methodology, commonly evaluated in settings that allow short selling, leverage, and frequent trading. Industry, on the other hand, operates under real constraints, but its data and methods are proprietary and largely unpublished. Neither is directly available to the private investor. This paper is an empirical study of established portfolio construction methods in the setting of the private investor. We consider a small investable universe of liquid US ETFs, where trading is monthly and carries a cost, and neither shorting nor leverage is permitted. Portfolio construction is posed as a convex optimization problem, its inputs are estimated from public data, and every parameter is interpretable. We denote such portfolios simple. We show that simple portfolios of as few as three ETFs deliver consistent and decent returns, without tuning to the backtest period. To find them, we have developed a framework, which we share publicly, able to backtest hundreds of portfolios on a standard laptop over a twenty year period or longer. When no return forecast is made, portfolios are constructed from risk alone, using methods such as risk parity and minimum volatility, built on a statistical factor model fitted with expectation maximization. When a forecast is made, we combine the Markowitz formulation with momentum signals and ridge regression. We report what works and what each component adds, weighing its gain against its complexity and the effort it demands of the investor. The findings are supported by numerical experiments over the past two decades, and the proposed portfolios outperform the standard 60/40 allocation.
papers.comment: 71 pages, 27 figures. Code available at https://github.com/AlexEmrik/consistent-decent-returns. Risk model package available at https://github.com/oskaredenwallberg/covforge and via pip install covforge

papers.title: Risk measures for infinite-server queues driven by a Cox-BESQ process
papers.summary: This paper introduces a model for infinite-server queues driven by a Cox process with stochastic intensity given by a squared Bessel (BESQ) process. Exploiting the affine structure of the underlying dynamics, we derive a closed-form expression for the joint moment-generating function (MGF) of the arrival intensity, the number of customers in the system, and the integral of the number of customers in the system over a time interval. This MGF can also be obtained at two (or more) dates, thereby allowing an analysis of the time evolution of infinite-server queues driven by a Cox--BESQ process. The availability of these explicit MGFs enables the development of risk measures for these variables, such as the joint moments of the arrival intensity, the number of customers in the system, and the integral of the number of customers in the system over a time interval, conditional on one of these variables exceeding a critical threshold. These risk measures can be determined at one or two dates. They rely essentially on the explicit form of the MGF of the state variables and on Fourier representations of the risk measures. Numerical experiments demonstrate the practical implementation of the proposed methodology and highlight the relevance of the theoretical results.

papers.title: The Term Structure of Implied Fee Rates in Liquidity Pools
papers.summary: We develop a no-arbitrage framework to recover implied fee rates from option-implied information and quantify fee compensation for liquidity providers in automated market maker (AMM) pools. Expected accumulated fees equal the current pool value minus the risk-neutral value of its terminal payoff, reducing forward-looking LP compensation to pricing the LP payoff. We apply the framework to Uniswap v2 and Uniswap v3 ETH--USDC pools using a stochastic-volatility jump-diffusion model calibrated to Deribit options. Implied fee rates are positive, time varying, downward sloping in maturity, and highly sensitive to range design, with tighter near-the-money ranges earning larger implied returns.

papers.title: Event definition and the branching ratio: Hawkes estimates of price-change clustering in the consolidated quote feed
papers.summary: Hawkes models of price changes in the consolidated US quote feed find a sub-millisecond kernel component and a branching ratio near criticality. We show that in large-tick stocks the first is the feed's construction: half of NBBO changes are locks or depleted quotes, resolved within a millisecond, which the model reads as excitation. Defining the event as a mid-price level persisting for one millisecond removes the component. Raw fits put three times the clean kernel mass within one second, which a simulation reproduces. Since the total branching ratio trades off against the baseline, we report kernel mass on a fixed window.

papers.title: Does Ecosystem Activity Validate TVL?
papers.summary: Total value locked (TVL) is widely used to assess decentralized finance ecosystems. Prior evidence finds that portfolios formed on TVL alone are spanned by the crypto market portfolio (Brigida 2025). This paper asks whether TVL becomes more informative when combined with measures of adoption, usage, development, protocol revenue, or social attention. I construct weekly value-weighted 2x3 portfolios that independently sort tokens on TVL-to-market-cap and one of seven ecosystem-activity ratios. Portfolio returns are computed from token prices using lagged-market-capitalization weights and evaluated against crypto market and size factors. Across the available 2022-2025 samples, none of the six on-chain double sorts rejects the benchmark after controlling for multiple testing. The same conclusion holds over 83 common weeks for which social-attention data are available. Several specifications reject at unadjusted levels, but none survives Holm adjustment. The social-attention rejection is only marginal under asymptotic inference and is insignificant under a moving-block bootstrap. Equal-weighted portfolios and formal parameter-stability tests lead to the same broad conclusion. The evidence therefore does not show that ecosystem activity reliably transforms TVL into an incremental return signal.

papers.title: Decorrelating the Advice Layer: A Calibrated Fragility Metric and Tested Mitigations for Synchronized Liquidation in Agentic Wealth Management
papers.summary: Conversational AI agents are turning wealth management into a continuous loop of market analysis, allocation, risk checks and execution, run for millions of clients on a handful of foundation models. We build a multi-asset agent-based model of this layer, calibrated to measured model concentration, cross-model correlation, retail turnover and 33 years of real equity returns, and ask when the layer amplifies market declines and what prevents it. The effective number of independent decision-makers is bounded however many clients the layer serves: about 2.0 at today's consumer concentration. This monoculture of views drives crowding in individual securities and sets the blast radius of a compromised model provider, but it does not drive market-wide liquidation. Index tail losses rise with the square root of agentic adoption, are 1.47-1.90 times larger under an agentic than under a periodic robo-advice architecture, and do not rise with model concentration; synchronized automation (risk overlays, drawdown cuts and attention-driven execution) drives them. A fragility index computed from aggregate flow, public returns and an impact estimate forecasts tail liquidation out of sample (hold-out R^2 of 0.56) far better than concentration or correlation measures. Decorrelating the automation, not the models, works: dispersing overlay parameters, staging execution and a participation breaker together cut tail liquidation by 63% at no measurable cost to client welfare, whereas provider diversification has no effect. Because the statistics required are sums, they can be computed across platforms under secure aggregation with differential privacy at negligible cost for realistic client populations. In historical replays, an agentic layer holding 10% of the market would have deepened the 2020 crash by about 858 basis points.

papers.title: FinLLM-KG: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced LLMs for Financial Sentiment Analysis in Algorithmic Trading
papers.summary: Recent advances in Generative AI have substantially improved financial sentiment analysis through post-trained financial large language models (LLMs). However, existing approaches remain confined to predicting the sentiment of each article in isolation and operate as black boxes, which limits contextual understanding and hinders deployment in high-stakes financial decision-making. To this end, we introduce FinLLM-KG, a model-agnostic framework that combines causal LLMs with a financial knowledge graph, in order to inject temporally grounded, company-level knowledge from SEC 10-K filings at inference time, without updating model weights. Within FinLLM-KG, context is supplied either as a natural-language company profile or as a small set of relevance-ranked factual triples. This enables sentiment predictions to account for broader firm-level information rather than the article alone, at almost zero computational cost and for any causal LLM. In addition, attributing each article-level sentiment score to individual sentences and to the retrieved knowledge-graph facts makes the evidence behind the prediction inspectable, thereby enhancing explainability and supporting human-in-the-loop review. Simulations demonstrate that FinLLM-KG consistently improves portfolio performance over the state-of-the-art baseline.

papers.title: Fuji: The Shape, Composition, and Spread of Demand Bursts on Robinhood Chain
papers.summary: Demand on blockchain-based marketplaces arrives in bursts and at a high rate. On these platforms the data are completely visible, which makes it feasible to compare the bursty demand against the usual load. The congestion manifests as an increased demand for gas, the primary resource a blockchain sells. Existing studies consider how to price the gas. The demand itself, and what it is made of during bursts, has not been measured. We measure it on Robinhood Chain, a layer-2 blockchain that quickly became a venue for trading tokenized equities and memecoins. We collected the data from every block of its first three active months and more than 50 million Uniswap swaps that occurred during bursty periods. We find that a burst trades about as many pools as a quiet period, mostly different ones, and trades them harder, on top of elevated demand that accumulated for hours. With the bursts aligned on their peaks, the median peak is 2.5 times the usual load. Both the rise and the fall of the demand are described by the sum of two exponential functions with different timescales, a slow one of hours and a fast one of minutes. Against a matched quiet period, a burst has 1.05 times the pools, 1.40 times the trades, and 1.21 times the senders. We use two models to explain the arrival of bursts: externally triggered cascades and self-excitation. The former fits the data relatively better. Inside a burst, the entry of each trader into a pool is followed for about 24 seconds by more entries than the existing traders predict. Whether this is because of imitation or because of a shared signal is left open.

papers.title: Weekend Crypto Volatility and Monday Market Risk
papers.summary: Cryptocurrencies trade continuously while major traditional markets close over the weekend. We examine whether weekend cryptocurrency volatility predicts Monday variance in equity, commodity and fixed-income markets. Using daily range-based variance measures for Bitcoin, Ether, XRP, the S&P 500, gold and a US Treasury ETF over 2017-2026, we augment heterogeneous autoregressive models with a common weekend cryptocurrency factor. Predictive content is weak before 2024 but significant thereafter. In the post-2024 sample, a one-standard-deviation increase in the factor is associated with 27-54% higher fitted Monday variance. Adding the factor reduces out-of-sample QLIKE losses by 11-22%, although statistical evidence varies across markets. Friday cryptocurrency volatility does not reproduce the result, and coin-specific variation adds no significant predictive information beyond the common factor. An endogenous procedure estimates a break in late 2023, during growing anticipation of US spot-Bitcoin ETF approval. However, ETF-flow interactions provide no evidence of amplification through greater measured Monday flow activity, leaving the mechanism unresolved. The findings suggest that calendar-specific volatility measures reveal predictive information that aggregate connectedness measures may obscure.

papers.title: Differentiability and Convexity of the Solution Maps for Fully Non-linear Parabolic HJB Equations
papers.summary: We study the dependence on the terminal condition of solutions to a fully nonlinear parabolic Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation, when the terminal condition varies along a finite-dimensional family. This problem is motivated by a dual formulation of semimartingale optimal transport. The equation is posed as a terminal-value Cauchy problem on an unbounded spatial domain. Under structural ellipticity and regularity assumptions on the nonlinear operator, we recall local parabolic Hölder estimates and stability results for bounded uniformly continuous terminal data. We then establish continuous directional differentiability of the solution map with respect to the finite-dimensional parameter, and identify its derivative through the corresponding linearized Cauchy problem. Under an additional convexity assumption on the Hamiltonian and a non-degeneracy condition on the terminal data, we prove local strong convexity of the point-evaluated solution map. The analysis relies on Evans--Krylov theory for fully nonlinear parabolic equations and combines PDE arguments with probabilistic representations. Finally, we extend the differentiability and convexity results to cascades of Cauchy problems in which successive equations are coupled through terminal conditions at several prescribed times. This structure is motivated, for instance, by optimal transport problems with marginal constraints imposed at several maturities.

papers.title: Scenario Matching for Credit Dependence Stress Tests: Temporal correlation constraints and empirical risk bounds
papers.summary: We couple two sets of simulated market and credit paths by minimizing absolute temporal-correlation error relative to a prescribed target. Each market path receives exactly one credit path, preserving both empirical distributions of complete scenarios. A perfect-matching test identifies whether a uniform correlation-error tolerance is feasible and determines its smallest attainable value. Further assignments give exact empirical mean-loss and exceedance-probability bounds; quantile bounds follow by binary search over eligible loss thresholds. A synthetic bond-forward credit stress test illustrates the method. The experiments report matching precision, empirical score tails and exposure-grid error, and measure matching and mean-loss computation. The method is independent of the scenario generator and provides a reproducible way to examine dependence assumptions in existing risk engines. Tail measures concern default-probability-weighted credit scores. Accompanying reproducibility package (Python code, synthetic scenario libraries, permutations, and benchmarks) is attached in the ZIP archive.

papers.title: Martingality in EFM Signature Volatility Models
papers.summary: We establish a martingality criterion for the Exponentially Fading Memory (EFM) signature volatility model, extending the recent result of Abi Jaber, Gassiat, and Sotnikov (2026). In the proposed framework, the volatility process is given by a linear functional of the EFM signature of a time-augmented Brownian motion, which yields a globally well-behaved, fully non-Markovian volatility model admitting a stationary distribution. The stationary EFM signature volatility model is also covered by allowing for a random initial value of the signature. Moreover, the volatility process can be adjusted to the initial forward variance curve. For this model, excluding trivial cases, we prove that the price process is a true martingale if and only if the truncation order is odd and a sign condition involving the correlation parameter holds.

papers.title: Det-MASO: Diversity-Regularized Multi-Agent Sequential Optimization for Factor Generation
papers.summary: Quantitative investment requires alpha factors that are both predictive and diverse. However, existing factor generation methods, including formulaic mining and neural end-to-end models, are mostly based on a single-agent design, which limits exploration of the factor space and reduces adaptability to changing markets. Multi-agent approaches can broaden exploration, but agents trained under a shared objective often collapse to similar outputs, while existing diversity techniques either scale poorly with asset-universe size or address redundancy only after training. We propose a multi-agent sequential optimization (Det-MASO) framework for generating diversified, context-adaptive alpha factors. It introduces a differentiable log-determinant penalty on the inter-agent correlation matrix directly into the joint objective, discouraging correlated agent behavior during training with computational cost that scales linearly with the number of assets. We further show that this penalty prevents homogeneous equilibria and preserves factor diversity throughout optimization, while a context-conditioned scheduler dynamically adjusts agent emphasis across market regimes and Shapley interaction index analysis is used to characterize the cooperation structure that emerges among them. Experiments show that Det-MASO outperforms baselines, improving the information coefficient by 1.1\%, the annualized return by 6.4\%, and the Sharpe ratio by 0.33.

papers.title: Do Round Numbers Hold Prices? Occupation Densities and Depth-Conditioned Hazards in the Limit Order Book
papers.summary: Prices cluster at round numbers, a pattern often interpreted as evidence that these levels act as price barriers. This pattern also admits a mechanical explanation: more liquidity rests there, and prices take longer to leave deeper queues. Limit order book data allow us to distinguish these mechanisms through a tick-grid framework in which local time counts departures and level-wise volatility reflects the departure hazard. Using data for five Nasdaq stocks throughout 2025, we find that round levels attract more liquidity but do not exhibit longer depth-adjusted durations. Intel and SoFi show directional effects, with departures biased away from round levels.

papers.title: Optimal ratcheting dividend policies with resets
papers.summary: We study an optimal dividend policy problem under ratcheting and bankruptcy constraints. Firms face a tradeoff between the negative signal of a dividend reduction and a potential future bankruptcy. In contrast to previous works, the dividend rate is allowed to decrease after incurring a negative impact on equity valuation in accordance with a large empirical literature on the topic. We provide an explicit necessary and sufficient condition for the finiteness of the value function and prove the differentiability of the value function, and its characterization via viscosity solutions and the so-called supercontact property. The value function is given by the solution of a two-dimensional variational inequality combining optimal stopping, singular and impulse controls. We show that the problem is equivalent to a one-dimensional setup simplifying both mathematical and financial analysis. Finally, we provide a numerical study of the model and a sensitivity analysis with respect to the model parameters. We show the relevance of over-reaction to financial news on the manager's optimal policy.

papers.title: Certifying Reward Alignment in Portfolio Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Financial reinforcement learning often translates an investment objective into an additive risk-adjusted reward. An agent can optimise that reward accurately yet implement a different financial preference. We develop a decision audit for terminal mean-variance equilibrium that separates reward misspecification from learning error. In a finite exogenous-state market, we bound the gain from changing one action using actor, reward and continuation-critic residuals. The certificate ignores state-constant critic offsets, accommodates convex action constraints, and has an independent-sample extension that does not require the equilibrium policy. A continuation-aware actor-critic method estimates the future-policy correction from samples. Across nine controlled markets and twenty seeds, it reduces policy distance by and one-step deviation gain by relative to a matched myopic-reward network. A separate PPO comparison tests the same reward intervention within a standard optimiser. Historical tests cross seven covariance estimators and 10, 30 and 49 US industry portfolios over 432 months: joint reward calibration preserves each fitted mean-variance target, but does not improve realised investment performance. Together, these results provide a way to quantify whether a learned decision implements its stated financial objective, separately from how well that objective performs in a backtest.
